However, their    autonomy, dynamic nature, and complex delegation relationships pose a    fundamental challenge to our existing authentication and    authorization frameworks, which were designed for human users and    traditional software.  This document dissects the novel    characteristics of AI Agents and outlines the new requirements for    authentication and authorization which can manage dynamic behavior    rather than verifying static identity.

name: draft-chen-oauth-agent-authz-use-cases
title: Agent Authorization use cases and gap analysis
abstract: This document provides a systematic analysis of these emerging agent-    based use cases.  It categorizes them into distinct scenarios,    details their specific authorization requirements, and performs a    comprehensive gap analysis against the existing OAuth 2.0    framework[RFC6749] and its common extensions.  The analysis    identifies fundamental gaps and requirements, providing a foundation    for future work on new extensions within the OAuth Working Group    toward creating a more secure and interoperable ecosystem for agent-    based systems.

name: draft-chen-oauth-agent-intent-token
title: The Intent Token - A Credential for Delegated User Intent
abstract: In the scenario of AI agent authorization, how to ensure that a    user's high-level, natural-language intent is correctly and safely    converted into low-level, specific authorization grants.  A    misunderstanding or malicious interpretation during this translation    can lead to significant security vulnerabilities.  This document    introduces the "Intent Token," a new type of security token designed    to bridge this semantic gap.  The Intent Token is a signed credential    that immutably captures the user's original intent.  It decouples the    act of granting an intent from the act of issuing specific access    tokens.  A client presents this Intent Token to an Authorization    Server, which acts as a trusted intermediary.  The Authorization    Server's responsibility is to interpret the user's stated intent and,    based on its policies, issue narrowly-scoped, short-lived access    tokens for specific resources, thereby ensuring the principle of    least privilege is upheld throughout the process.

name: draft-chen-oauth-agent-revocation
title: OAuth 2.0 Agent Authorization Explicit Revocation
abstract: The OAuth 2.0 Token Revocation mechanism defined in RFC 7009 enables    clients to notify authorization servers that a token is no longer    needed.  However, that mechanism is limited to single-token    operations and does not support batch revocation, cascade    propagation, or context-aware semantics at the agent level.  With the    emergence of autonomous systems and cross-domain agent networks,    authorization servers require more granular, traceable revocation    semantics.     This document defines an agent-based explicit revocation extension,    introducing new endpoints, request/response formats, and coordination    protocols to support batch revocation based on agent IDs, cascade    propagation, conditional revocation, and verifiable audit trails.

name: draft-chen-oauth-rar-agent-extensions
title: Policy, Lifecycle, and Intent Extensions for OAuth Rich Authorization Requests
abstract: OAuth 2.0 Rich Authorization Requests (RAR) [RFC9396] defines a    syntax for clients to request fine-grained permissions.  While    powerful, this mechanism lacks standardized methods for clients to    express three critical contextual dimensions prevalent in modern    automated systems: the high-level user intent driving the request,    the required security policy under which the request should be    evaluated, and the binding of the authorization's lifecycle to an    external process.     This document extends the RAR framework to address these gaps.  It    first defines a new authorization_details type, *intent_request*, to    facilitate goal-oriented authorization.  Second, it introduces two    new parameters for the authorization_details object:    *policy_context*, to request authorization under a specific assurance    level, and *lifecycle_binding*, to tie the validity of the    authorization grant to the state of an external entity.  These    extensions enable authorization servers to make more intelligent,    secure, and context-aware decisions, particularly in ecosystems    involving autonomous agents and complex, long-running tasks.

name: draft-chen-oauth-scope-agent-extensions
title: Structured and Constraint Extensions for OAuth Scopes
abstract: This specification defines an extension to the OAuth 2.0 scope    parameter, as specified in RFC 6749, which is used to express the    permissions granted to an access token.  The proposed extension    introduces a structured syntax for scope values to enable fine-    grained authorization for the installation and execution of Modular    Capability Units (encapsulated and reusable functional modules such    as skills) within Agent ecosystems.  However, current mechanisms for    authorizing such modules generally lack a standardized way to express    and obtain consent for the complex, fine-grained permissions they    require during installation.     This document addresses this limitation by defining a structured    format for the scope parameter.  The format extends the simple space-    delimited strings with a colon-separated syntax:    [resource_type]:[action]:[target][:constraints].  This syntax allows    for the precise description of permissions for operations such as    file system access, command-line execution, network access, tool    invocation, and scheduled tasks.  These extensions provide a    standardized, machine-readable way to request, convey, and validate    detailed permissions, thereby enhancing users' security control over    their resources while maintaining compatibility with the existing    OAuth token issuance and validation flows.

name: draft-chen-pcp-discovery-llmnr
title: Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution (LLMNR) Deployment Consideration for PCP Server Discovery
abstract: The memo has recommended to deploy Link-Local Multicast Name    Resolution (LLMNR) in PCP scenarioes.  Depending on that, it could    not only avoid adherence to DNS during PCP server name resolving, but    also company with PCP FQDN DHCP options extention to accomplish PCP    server discovery.  In order to fit LLMNR into PCP network, particular    LLMNR deployment guide and relevant configurations are considerated    along with PCP elements installation.

name: draft-cheng-rtgwg-ai-network-reliability-problem
title: Reliability in AI Networks Gap Analysis, Problem Statement, and Requirements
abstract: This document provides the gap analysis of existing reliability    mechanism in AI networks, describes the fundamental problems, and    defines the requirements for technical improvements.

name: draft-cheng-spring-srv6-for-ai-network
title: A SRv6 Traffic Engineering Application for AI Network
abstract: AI applications require fast processing and responses. Traffic using    RoCEv2 has low entropy for ECMP. At the same time, AI elephant flows    are predictable. Traffic engineering technology for AI backend    networks becomes a possible solution. SRv6 TE can start from the    host side, making SRv6 source routing and traffic path control from    the host side an optional solution.     This document presents a AI network Traffic Engineering (TE)    application scenario for handling link faults and traffic congestion    issues in data centers, based on Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6)    and Compressed Segment Identifier (CSID). The application scenario    uses SRv6 CSID Network Programming to directly install all    forwarding paths on the head-end device. When a data center    experiences a link fault or traffic congestion, the head-end device    switches the forwarding path to another optimal path for avoiding    the location of link fault or traffic congestion, ensuring optimal    AI data flow forwarding.

name: draft-chowdhury-dhc-mip6-agentop
title: DHCP Relay Agent Option to Support Mobile IPv6 bootstrapping
abstract: This document defines a new DHCPv6 option and number of sub-options     for DHCP Relay Agent to facilitate Mobile IPv6 bootstrapping along     with a AAA infrastructure.

name: draft-chuang-agent-attribution-header-fields
title: Agent Attribution Header Fields
abstract: When human users communicate with autonomous computer agent users,    the human users should be able to identify that communication as    coming from agent users and know which humans are responsible for the    agent users.  This document specifies email header fields that an    email sender can use to transmit agent user attribution information    to email receivers.  The first header field is human readable and    specifies the agent's responsible humans' email address.  The second    header field is machine readable and specified in JSON attribution    information.

name: draft-chuyi-nmrg-agentic-network-inference
title: Agentic Network Architecture and Protocol for Supporting Agent Interconnection Communication and Multi-level Inference
abstract: With the advent of the era of AI large models and intelligent agents,    more and more scenarios about agent interconnection have emerged,    such as collaboration among multiple agents within a household,    intelligent robots cooperating to complete pipeline tasks in    different operations of the industrial Internet, drone groups,    intelligent vehicle networking, etc.  These scenarios not only    require low latency and high bandwidth, but also demand efficient    information exchange and cross-domain coordination and scheduling    capabilities in complex collaborative tasks.  Therefore, new    orchestration and management technologies and frameworks are needed    in existing networks to address this.  The interconnection of    different agents also brings about an emergence of inference, with a    large number of inference requests being processed from the mobile    phone side to the cloud.  In order to improve inference efficiency,    in a cloud-edge-end multi-layer inference architecture, large models    and agents at different levels cooperate to complete tasks, resulting    in a complex intelligent agent interconnection network.  Gateways and    routers serve as forwarding entries on the network road highways,    responsible for building communication channels for the agents spread    throughout the network, which requiring function upgrades to support    the continuously evolving inference service in the future.

name: draft-chuyi-nmrg-ai-agent-network
title: Large Model based Agents for Network Operation and Maintenance
abstract: Current advancements in AI technologies, particularly large models,    have demonstrated immense potential in content generation, reasoning,    analysis and so on, providing robust technical support for network    automation and self-intelligence.  However, in practical network    operations, challenges such as system isolation and fragmented data    lead to extensive manual, repetitive, and inefficient tasks, the    improvement of intelligence level is very necessary.  This document    identifies typical scenarios requiring enhanced intelligence, and    explains how AI Agents and large model technologies can empower    networks to address operational pain points, reduce manual efforts,    and explore impacts on network data, system architectures, and    interfaces correspondingly.  It further explores and summarizes    standardization efforts in implementation.

name: draft-condrey-rats-witnessd-enrollment
title: Trust Anchor Bootstrap Protocol for Proof of Process
abstract: This document specifies a trust anchor bootstrap protocol for the    witnessd Proof of Process framework.  The protocol defines how new    devices enter the witnessd ecosystem, how device keys are provisioned    and verified, and how Verifiers discover and validate device trust    anchors.     Three enrollment modes are defined: self-sovereign mode for    individual users, organizational mode for enterprise deployments, and    public registry mode for federated trust ecosystems.

name: draft-contario-totp-secure-enrollment
title: TOTP Secure Enrollment
abstract: This document describes a secure key exchange scheme that extends the    Time-Based One-Time Password (TOTP) [RFC6238] de facto enrollment    method to prevent compromise of the non-expiring TOTP key by    photographic capture of the QR code or by intentional or    unintentional persistence of the key string in email, SMS, or other    systems outside of the TOTP authenticator system itself.

name: draft-contreras-bmwg-ai-agent-benchmarking
title: Benchmarking Methodology for AI Agents in Network Operations
abstract: This document defines a benchmarking methodology for evaluating    Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents performing network operations    tasks such as configuration, troubleshooting, and optimization.  This    document focuses on task-oriented performance metrics, including task    completion success, execution efficiency, and robustness across    multi-step workflows, proposing benchmarking practices towards agent-    based, closed-loop network operation scenarios.     The proposed methodology aims to provide a reproducible and vendor-    independent framework to compare AI agent effectiveness in controlled    network environments.

name: draft-contreras-bpm-ai-agent-benchmarking
title: Benchmarking Methodology for AI Agents in Network Operations
abstract: This document defines a benchmarking methodology for evaluating    Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents performing network operations    tasks such as configuration, troubleshooting, and optimization.  This    document focuses on task-oriented performance metrics, including task    completion success, execution efficiency, and robustness across    multi-step workflows, proposing benchmarking practices towards agent-    based, closed-loop network operation scenarios.     The proposed methodology aims to provide a reproducible and vendor-    independent framework to compare AI agent effectiveness in controlled    network environments.

name: draft-corneo-t2trg-sdf-coap-agents
title: Extending SDF and CoAP for AI Agent Interaction with IoT Devices
abstract: This document proposes extensions to the Semantic Definition Format    (SDF) and the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) to better    support AI agent interaction with Internet of Things (IoT) devices.    It covers two aspects: identifying AI agents in CoAP transactions,    and making SDF device descriptions readily consumable by large    language models (LLMs) and autonomous agents.  The document is    intended to stimulate discussion within T2TRG on these topics.

name: draft-cui-ai-agent-discovery-invocation
title: AI Agent Discovery and Invocation Protocol
abstract: This document proposes a standardized protocol for discovery and    invocation of AI agents.  It defines a common metadata format for    describing AI agents (including capabilities, I/O specifications,    supported languages, tags, authentication methods, etc.), a    capability-based discovery mechanism, and a unified RESTful    invocation interface.     This revision refines the discovery mechanism by defining fields for    intent-based agent selection.  This capability enables a client, host    agent, or orchestration system to describe a task intent and receive    a ranked set of candidate agents before invocation, without changing    existing discovery or invocation semantics.     The goal is to enable cross-platform interoperability among AI agents    by providing a discover-and-match mechanism and a unified invocation    entry point.  Security considerations, including authentication and    trust measures, are also discussed.  This specification aims to    facilitate the formation of multi-agent systems by making it easy to    find the right agent for a task and invoke it in a consistent manner    across different vendors and platforms.  Intent-based selection is an    application-layer capability and does not define network routing,    packet forwarding, path computation, reachability advertisement, or    address resolution.

name: draft-cui-ai-agent-task
title: Task-oriented Coordination Requirements for AI Agent Protocols
abstract: AI agent communication requires intelligent task level coordination    to manage dynamic workloads across large-scale, heterogeneous    networking environments.  This draft proposes general requirements    for an agent protocol to enable autonomous task coordination at    scale, including dynamic task discovery, negotiation, and context-    aware scheduling with real-time adaptability.

name: draft-cui-dawn-cooperating-discovery
title: Resource Discovery in Cooperating Domains
abstract: This document specifies a mechanism for resource discovery across    cooperating administrative domains.  It defines how discovery    requests preserve their scope and constraints across referrals, how    discovery services report coverage of requested scopes, and how    clients combine results from multiple discovery branches.  The    mechanism enables clients to distinguish complete discovery results    from incomplete operations, including cases involving unresolved    referrals, pagination failures, and partial service failures.  It    relies on existing authentication, authorization, and trust    arrangements and does not define open-ended Internet search, semantic    matchmaking, resource invocation, registration, or directory    synchronization.

name: draft-cui-dawn-local-llm-api-discovery
title: Discovery of LLM API Services in Local Networks
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) API services can be hosted on    workstations, local servers, and other devices in a local network.    AI applications commonly access these services through manually    configured API base URLs and interface settings.  When an application    joins a different network or a service address changes, these    settings may need to be updated even when a suitable local service is    already available.     This document specifies a DNS-Based Service Discovery (DNS-SD)    profile for discovering LLM API services on a local link.  An    advertiser publishes the service location and a small set of API    connection parameters.  A discovery client resolves these records and    offers the resulting connection information to an AI application or    its configuration adapter.  Subsequent LLM API requests are sent    directly to the discovered service, not through the advertiser or    discovery client.  Discovery does not establish trust, distribute    credentials, select models, or define an application's configuration    file format.

name: draft-cui-dawn-mdi-model
title: Minimum Public Discovery Information: Requirements and Common Semantics
abstract: The charter of the Discovery of Agents With Names (DAWN) working    group asks it to specify the minimum public discovery information    that a client obtains when it discovers an AI resource.  An    individual draft on DAWN terminology defines Minimum Discoverable    Information (MDI) as the minimum amount of information an entity    needs to provide to become discoverable, distinguishes it from the    Minimum Viable Dataset (MVD) that a discovery mechanism needs as    input, and gives only examples of the content of either.  Individual    drafts on the DAWN problem statement and requirements call for a    standardized minimum structure and list what it must at least    contain; in its absence, emerging discovery formats risk each    defining its own minimal metadata, with descriptors that do not    interoperate across organizational or protocol boundaries.     This document addresses the minimum public discovery information as a    client obtains it and as a publisher provides it, and its relation to    the input of discovery; registration mechanisms are outside its    scope.  Using the distinction RFC 3444 draws between information    models and data models, it describes the information involved in    publication, lookup, and response; proposes a procedure that derives    what is minimal for each deployment context from the scope of the    charter; applies the procedure to the charter's three deployment    contexts: a local network, an organization, and the domain of a    cooperating party; and proposes a set of elements with the minimal    constraints that hold among them.  Information can be supplied by the    discovery response, by context the client already has, or by binding    rules.  This document is input to the DAWN architecture and protocol    work; normative definitions that affect interoperability belong to    the corresponding Standards Track documents.  It is a mapping target    for richer descriptors.

name: draft-cui-dmsc-agent-cdi
title: Cross-Domain Interoperability Framework for AI Agent Collaboration
abstract: This document defines a framework for enabling seamless cross-domain    interoperability among AI agents operating across different networks,    administrative domains, and heterogeneous platforms.  The framework    addresses the challenges of identity federation, trust establishment,    policy harmonization, and secure communication that arise when AI    agents from distinct administrative realms need to collaborate on    shared tasks.  It specifies mechanisms for agent discovery,    capability negotiation, trust delegation, and federated policy    enforcement, enabling scalable and secure multi-domain AI    collaboration without requiring centralized control.

name: draft-cui-dns-native-agent-naming-resolution
title: DNS-Native AI Agent Naming and Resolution
abstract: This document specifies DNS-Native Agent Naming and Resolution (DN-    ANR) for AI agents.  DN-ANR uses domain names (FQDNs) as stable Agent    Identifiers and resolves a selected Agent Identifier to verifiable    endpoints and supported protocol/version information with a    cryptographic integrity chain, with DNSSEC preferred.     DN-ANR is a post-selection resolution profile.  It does not define    agent discovery, capability search, semantic matching, ranking, or    routing decisions.  Agent discovery, publication, or registry,    including DNS-based mechanisms such as DNS-AID, may produce candidate    Agent Identifiers; DN-ANR resolves and verifies the identifier    selected by such mechanisms or by local policy.  Within that scope,    DN-ANR additionally defines DNS-based version distribution and    deterministic version selection, canonicalized SVCB integrity cross-    checking, and a signed HTTPS mirror for clients that cannot perform    SVCB queries.  While AI agents are the primary use case, the    resolution and verification behavior defined here applies to any    entity identified by an FQDN, such as services and workloads.

name: draft-cui-netext-route-optimization-agent-ext
title: Reflector Extension for Route Optimization Agent
abstract: Route Optimization is a very useful feature in Mobile IPv6. Mobile  node can communicate with correspondent node without the involvement  of the home agent in Route Optimization mode. But there are some  limitations to this feature. One problem is that the mobile node and  the correspondent node must be capable for Route Optimization. This  document introduces a Route Optimization Agent function used for  Route Optimization and this extension mechanism can enable Route  Optimization mode to be used between mobile node and simple IP node.  In the extension solution, the Route Optimization Agent function may  be implemented in LMA or MAG and the Agent entity can reflect the   RO-related signal messages and accomplish the Route Optimization  procedure on behalf of the simple IP node.         Conventions used in this document   The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT",  "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this  document are to be interpreted as described in [RFC2119].

name: draft-cui-nmop-agent-sketch-com
title: Operational Requirements for Network State Exchange in Agent-Assisted Network Operations
abstract: This document describes operational requirements for exchanging    network state in agent-assisted network operations.  In this    document, an agent-assisted system is any automation or decision-    support system that consumes operational state to support tasks such    as anomaly triage, incident correlation, configuration verification,    traffic engineering analysis, or attack mitigation support.  Such a    system may use a large language model (LLM), a rule engine, a    statistical model, or conventional software.     The document focuses on operational problems created by high-volume    telemetry, cross-domain state sharing, privacy constraints,    approximate state summaries, and auditability of state used by    automated workflows.  It identifies requirements for compact, scoped,    mergeable, bounded-error, incrementally synchronized, and auditable    network state artifacts.  The document complements existing NMOP work    on anomaly detection, incident management, and YANG Push/message    broker integration.  It does not define a new network management    protocol, a new agent communication protocol, or a wire format.

name: draft-cui-nmrg-llm-benchmark
title: A Framework to Evaluate LLM Agents for Network Configuration
abstract: This document specifies an evaluation framework and related    definitions for intent-driven network configuration using Large    Language Model(LLM)-based agents.  The framework combines an    emulator-based interactive environment, a suite of representative    tasks, and multi-dimensional metrics organized in two layers: outcome    metrics that verify functional correctness in a method-agnostic way,    and agentic process metrics that assess reasoning quality and    interactive command generation.  Functional testcase results serve as    the primary metric; command and reasoning scores act as diagnostic    estimates against the task's ground truth configurations (which may    include more than one validated solution), and optional efficiency    metrics capture time and token cost.  The framework aims to enable    reproducible, comprehensive, and fair comparisons among network    configuration approaches, covering both agentic and non-agentic    solutions while highlighting capabilities specific to autonomous    agents.

name: draft-cui-nmrg-llm-nm
title: A Framework for LLM Agent-Assisted Network Management with Human-in-the-Loop
abstract: This document describes a reference framework for collaborative    network management between Large Language Model (LLM)-assisted agents    and human operators.  Because network management actions can affect    service availability, security posture, customer traffic, and    compliance obligations, LLM-generated recommendations need to be    validated, reviewed, and audited before they are applied to    operational networks.  The framework therefore focuses on human-in-    the-loop control for safe, auditable, and operator-supervised use of    LLM-assisted decision support in network operations.  The document is    intended to be compatible with existing network management systems    and protocols while identifying research issues, rather than    specifying a complete implementation of all LLM agent mechanisms.

name: draft-cui-semantic-routing-ai-agent-communication
title: Semantic Routing for AI Agent Communication
abstract: AI agents often know the intended outcome of a task without knowing    which agent, model, tool, workflow, or service should process it.    This document describes an application-layer semantic routing    framework that selects one Processing Target from task intent,    execution context, target capabilities, constraints, and local    policy.  It defines a common operation-level information model and    externally observable selection behavior that protocol bindings can    preserve.  Semantic matching is implementation-specific.  This    document does not define task decomposition, multi-agent    orchestration, network-layer routing, target discovery, target    invocation, or a new agent communication protocol.

name: draft-daniel-ai-agent-internet-architecture
title: Architectural Requirements for Supporting AI Agents on the Internet
abstract: Autonomous AI agents are evolving from interactive assistants into    networked software workloads that discover services, invoke tools,    delegate authority, transact, communicate with other agents, and act    asynchronously on behalf of humans and organizations.  Existing    Internet protocols provide strong foundations, but agent autonomy,    dynamic delegation, machine-speed execution, long and unpredictable    model-processing intervals, and cross-domain interaction create    requirements that span multiple protocol families.     This document describes architectural requirements for supporting AI    agents on the Internet across naming and discovery, HTTP,    authentication, authorization and delegation, TLS and workload    identity, transport and connection continuity, asynchronous    messaging, capability and intent-based resolution, payments,    provenance, auditability, revocation, security, and privacy.  It    favors profiling and extending existing Internet protocols over    defining a monolithic new agent protocol, and identifies the need for    IETF-wide architectural coordination.

name: draft-das-agent-credential-privacy
title: Secure AI Execution-Finality for iOS, Android, and Cross-Platform AI Agents, Part 9: Credential Custody, Operation-Bound Secret Use, and Protected Data Disclosure
abstract: Giving an AI agent a credential usually means giving it everything    that credential can do.  When Apple Siri, Google Gemini, enterprise    copilots, coding agents, or third-party AI tools act with a user's    OAuth tokens, API keys, signing keys, or logged-in sessions on iOS,    iPadOS, macOS, Android, cloud APIs, developer tools, financial    services, and telecom systems, a prompt-injected or confused agent    can export data, call APIs, sign transactions, write poisoned entries    into its own long-term memory, or leak information piece by piece to    different recipients. iOS Keychain and the Secure Enclave, Android    Keystore, sandboxing, token authentication, proof of possession, and    a successful approval each protect something real, but none of them    establishes authority for the exact outgoing data, recipient, or    resource effect.     This document, Part 9 of a twelve-part series, specifies how    credentials and data are used only for the specific operation that    was authorized.  It describes protected secret custody in which the    agent never receives the raw secret; operation-bound credential    activation; continuity of credential generation and source authority    across key and token rotation; independent Finality Sink inspection    of the real outgoing request; recipient-scoped, cumulative,    correlation-aware disclosure accounting, including derived summaries;    provenance of source-derived information; retrieval-time provenance    and write authority for agent memory and retrieval-augmented    generation stores; and non-replayable consumption of finality.  It    does not assume that a third-party mobile application can mediate    other applications without their cooperation.  Reference algorithms,    fourteen threat models, and thirty-two reproducible tests, including    current Android and iOS authorized-call cases, are included.  Part 1    of the series defines the shared terminology and common workflows.     The document relates these mechanisms to OAuth 2.0 Rich Authorization    Requests, Resource Indicators, Token Exchange, Demonstrating Proof of    Possession (DPoP), and mutual-TLS sender constraints; the Workload    Identity in Multi-System Environments (WIMSE) architecture and the    WIMSE working group's AI Identity Management System draft on agent    authentication and authorization; Authentication and Authorization    for Constrained Environments (ACE); CBOR Object Signing and    Encryption (COSE); Remote ATtestation procedureS (RATS); Supply Chain    Integrity, Transparency, and Trust (SCITT); and HTTP semantics.    These are treated as qualified inputs rather than final authority,    without claiming working-group adoption or IETF consensus.     Industry alignment covers Apple iOS, iPadOS, and macOS with Siri,    Keychain, Secure Enclave, and App Intents; Google Android with    Gemini, Keystore, app permissions, and inter-process communication;    Samsung Bixby, Microsoft Copilot, and Amazon Alexa; Microsoft Windows    and Azure; Amazon Web Services and other cloud identity platforms;    cloud key-management and hardware security module signing services;    agent platforms from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta; Model    Context Protocol connectors and their OAuth-based authorization;    passkeys and WebAuthn; password managers and autofill; enterprise    SaaS connectors; open banking and consent-based data sharing,    including India's Account Aggregator framework; digital wallets and    payment APIs; healthcare data; human-resources and recruiting agents;    source-code secrets and CI/CD; personal assistant memory; advertising    and analytics data sharing; the EU Digital Identity Wallet; NVIDIA,    Qualcomm, Arm, and Huawei hardware; telecommunications messaging; RAG    and vector databases; and public-sector systems.  For each, the    document states the technical effect: a secret is exercised, or data    is released, only for the specific authorized operation and    recipient, and only within the remaining disclosure budget.  Product    names are illustrative and imply no endorsement or implementation by    any vendor.  For the EU Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation (EU)    2024/1689), and alongside data-protection-by-design obligations under    the General Data Protection Regulation, operation-bound credential    use and recipient-scoped disclosure records can help providers and    deployers address cybersecurity, record-keeping, and risk-management    requirements where those obligations apply; this is a technical    mapping, not a conformity claim or legal advice.

name: draft-das-agent-execution-finality
title: Protected Execution-Finality Architecture for AI and Autonomous Systems: Act-Bound Capabilities and Effectuation-Boundary Verification
abstract: This document describes a proposed protected execution-finality    architecture for artificial-intelligence agents, autonomous software    systems, confidential computing environments, and distributed    execution infrastructures.  The architecture addresses a fundamental    security distinction: the ability of an AI agent or computational    process to generate, prepare, or request an operation does not    independently establish the protected authority required to make that    operation effective.     The proposed architecture separates the computation plane from    protected execution authority through mandatory operation    interception, Non-Effective State staging, machine-verifiable    Candidate Act Descriptors, a Protected Enforcement Domain (PED),    protected authorization-state management, scoped non-bearer execution    capabilities, and Finality Sink verification.  A Candidate Act    remains non-effective until the applicable authority, purpose,    destination, execution scope, runtime context, policy epoch,    freshness, revocation, and other mandatory authorization predicates    have been validated.  Where required, protected validation evidence    is committed before, or atomically with, capability availability.    The designated Finality Sink independently verifies the capability    against the actual operation and applicable protected state    immediately before permitting the governed consequential effect.     The architecture addresses AI-agent sandbox isolation, mandatory and    non-bypassable mediation, out-of-process permission authorities,    executable-specific access restrictions, network and API egress    enforcement, destination resolution, redirect consistency, credential    brokering, protected credential substitution, privileged connectors,    human and developer approval, runtime policy modification, multi-    agent delegation, taint and provenance-based authorization, and fail-    closed execution control.     For technical discoverability and independent architectural    examination, related publicly documented industry systems include    Meta Muse/Sentinel and NVIDIA OpenShell, NemoClaw, and the Open Agent    Safety Platform/Sentry.  Relevant engineering terminology includes    Muse Secure VM, isolated runtime cells, host-side permission    authority, forward proxies, surrogate credentials, just-in-time    credential insertion, eBPF/LSM-based taint propagation, controlled    network egress, executable-specific policy enforcement, developer-    approved policy changes, and hardware-assisted monitoring through    SmartNICs, data processing units, BlueField, and DOCA.  These    references identify relevant public engineering contexts and    functional security objectives; they do not establish that the named    systems implement the complete architecture described here.     The principal technical distinction examined in this document    concerns the relationship between an upstream permission decision and    independently enforceable authority at the actual effectuation    boundary.  The proposed execution-finality sequence includes    protected validation of a concrete Candidate Act, required protected-    state handling, validation-evidence commitment, operation-bound    capability release, and mandatory verification of that capability by    the applicable Finality Sink.  The architecture distinguishes    conventional permission checking, credential isolation, model-    computation admission, and post-event monitoring or quarantine from    the separate authorization conditions required before an externally    consequential operation becomes effective.     The document further describes enforcement across network gateways,    host operating systems, credential-release interfaces, service    meshes, autonomous code-deployment systems, confidential virtual    machines, protected storage, database commitments, accelerator    fabrics, DMA/RDMA transfers, SmartNICs, DPUs, hardware Finality    Latches, and receiving-side execution boundaries.  It addresses    protected state consumption, capability replay prevention, policy-    version fencing, distributed revocation, hardware attestation,    workload migration, snapshot rollback, crash-consistent recovery, and    prevention of unauthorized duplicate effects.  Authorization of one    effectuation boundary does not automatically establish authority for    a distinct downstream consequence.     This individual Informational Internet-Draft presents architectural    mechanisms, enforcement points, implementation alternatives, and    security considerations for independent technical examination.  It    does not specify a complete interoperable wire protocol or request    IANA allocations.  Industry and product names are used solely for    technical relevance, terminology identification, and discoverability,    without implying affiliation, endorsement, copying, derivation,    infringement, patent validity, or architectural identity.     Related Indian Patent Disclosures and Claimed Priority: The author    identifies Indian Application No. 202531130665, dated 23 December    2025, as an earlier related foundational disclosure, together with    Indian provisional applications 202631000572 (3 January 2026),    202631001586 (7 January 2026), and 202631002990 (12 January 2026)    concerning execution-time authorization and irreversible-boundary    enforcement.  Indian Application No. 202631124028 is separately    identified as a related patent-pending application.     Related International Patent Applications and WIPO Publications: The    author identifies PCT/IB2025/058316 (Mothership; WO 2025/210622),    PCT/IB2026/053385 (ALF-PCT; WO 2026/115520), PCT/IB2026/055615 (DAS    Protocols I; WO 2026/150382), PCT/IB2026/055760 (DAS Protocols II; WO    2026/150383), PCT/IB2026/055870 (DAS Protocols III; WO 2026/150384),    PCT/IB2026/056058 (DAS Protocols IV; WO 2026/154461), PCT/    IB2026/056809 (DAS Protocols V; WO 2026/172334), and PCT/    IB2026/056941 (DAS Protocols VI; WO 2026/172336) as related technical    disclosures.     These application identifiers and publication references are provided    to facilitate independent examination of the original technical    documents and their chronology.  Any claimed priority entitlement    depends upon the actual subject-matter support contained in the    corresponding earlier filing and the applicable legal requirements.    The filing chronology does not imply that every technical mechanism    described in this Internet-Draft was disclosed in every earlier    application.     Fundamental architectural principle: Computation is not authority to    act.

name: draft-das-agent-tool-integrity
title: Secure AI Execution-Finality for iOS, Android, and Cross-Platform AI Agents, Part 7: AI Tool Integrity, Semantic Target Correspondence, and Execution-Time Resource Identity
abstract: An AI agent can call the right tool with valid credentials and still    act on the wrong thing.  When a user tells Apple Siri or Google    Gemini to "send this to her", asks a coding agent to deploy, or lets    a browser agent complete a form, the agent must resolve which file,    contact, account, tenant, or device is meant, and which tool, tool    version, and model will act.  On iOS, iPadOS, macOS, Android,    Windows, Linux, enterprise SaaS, cloud platforms, and connected    hardware, agents can select the wrong user-referenced object, follow    instructions injected into web pages, repositories, or tool outputs,    call a tool whose description or capabilities silently changed, run    on a swapped model or configuration, or send authorized-looking    requests to redirected hosts, rebound aliases, and substituted    tenants.  Identity authentication, sandboxing, and transport    encryption can all succeed while files, credentials, payments,    developer infrastructure, and physical devices are exposed.     This document, Part 7 of a twelve-part series, specifies execution-    time integrity for AI tools.  It describes protected correspondence    between what the user saw and referred to and the object actually    acted on; canonical tool-effect contracts with semantic-compatibility    checks across tool versions; algorithm, model, and configuration    baseline continuity; instruction provenance with evaluation of lower-    trust influence on downstream actions; authenticated resolution of    resource aliases, hosts, and tenants, including redirects and DNS    rebinding; fencing of tool installation, activation, runtime upgrade,    and rollback; detection of dynamic service and capability    substitution; and reconstruction of the actual operation at an    independent Finality Sink.  Reference algorithms, twelve threat    models, and thirty reproducible tests, including iOS App Intents and    Android cooperating-app cases, are included.  Part 1 of the series    defines the shared terminology and common workflows.     The document relates these mechanisms to OAuth 2.0 authorization,    Rich Authorization Requests, Resource Indicators, Token Exchange, and    Demonstrating Proof of Possession (DPoP); Workload Identity in Multi-    System Environments (WIMSE); Remote ATtestation procedureS (RATS);    CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE); Supply Chain Integrity,    Transparency, and Trust (SCITT); Software Updates for Internet of    Things (SUIT) manifests; Trusted Execution Environment Provisioning    (TEEP); Authentication and Authorization for Constrained Environments    (ACE); and HTTP redirect and conditional-request semantics.  None of    these alone is treated as conferring final authority for a    consequential effect, and no working-group adoption or IETF consensus    is claimed.     Industry alignment covers Apple iOS, iPadOS, and macOS with Siri,    Shortcuts, App Intents, and Keychain; Google Android with Gemini,    intents, Binder, and Keystore; Samsung Bixby, Microsoft Copilot, and    Amazon Alexa; Microsoft Windows and Azure; coding and computer-use    agents from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta; Model Context    Protocol servers, agent-to-agent protocols, and tool and plugin    registries; browser agents; NVIDIA, Qualcomm, Arm, and Huawei    hardware; banking, payments, and agentic commerce; email and    messaging agents; healthcare record agents; document signing; cloud    infrastructure-as-code; model hosting and model routing; smart homes    using Matter; automotive assistants and over-the-air updates;    government digital identity, including the EU Digital Identity    Wallet; telecommunications; industrial IoT and robotics; and software    supply chains and CI/CD.  For each, the document states the technical    effect: the consequential operation reaches the Finality Sink only if    the actual target, tool contract, model baseline, and instruction    lineage match what was authorized.  Product names are illustrative    and imply no endorsement or implementation by any vendor.  For the EU    Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), execution-    time integrity of tools, models, and targets can help providers and    deployers address accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity, record-    keeping, and risk-management requirements where those obligations    apply; this is a technical mapping, not a conformity claim or legal    advice.

name: draft-das-agentic-adaptive-authorization
title: Adaptive Authorization for Agentic AI: Graduated and Escalated Execution Control for Critical Infrastructure
abstract: AI agents are beginning to move money, release confidential data,    change cloud privileges, and command industrial and other critical-    infrastructure equipment.  Existing controls answer whether an actor    or request may proceed.  These include authentication, OAuth scopes,    conditional access, risk engines, and attestation.  None of them,    alone, guarantees three things about the consequence that finally    occurs: that it is the exact act that was evaluated, that it is still    permitted under current state, and that it cannot be replayed,    substituted, or routed around the check.  Risk engines that return    ESCALATE widen this gap.  The escalation is a label, and nothing    forces the stricter conditions it implies to reach the point where    the effect actually happens.     This document defines Graduated and Escalated Conditional Execution    Finality.  Every AI-generated operation is held as a non-effective    Candidate Act. It is classified into a graduated release class rather    than a binary allow/deny: ordinary, reduced, escalated, canary,    sandbox, review, quarantine, or deny.  For an elevated-risk act, the    system first derives a narrower consequence boundary.  It then binds    the required controls into an act-bound, sink-bound Execution Handle;    examples include a lower value, one named recipient, protected    approval, short validity, fresh attestation, and single use.  The    Finality Sink at the last preventable boundary re-verifies those    controls against current protected state, atomically with    effectuation.     The contribution is threefold.  First, escalation changes executable    authority, not merely a decision record.  Second, escalation is    monotonic: it cannot be laundered, fragmented, downgraded, or    resubmitted away on its path to the sink.  Third, the Finality Sink    is shown to be necessary but not sufficient, so finality is an end-    to-end property rather than a gateway.  The document specifies    nineteen testable enforcement points, from the base execution-    dependency mechanism to proxy, hardware, escrow, rollback,    inheritance, and path-closure requirements.  It also provides a    comparison with conventional mechanisms, a security model with    explicit assumptions and invariants, a latency model, escalation-    specific attacks, and the problems it leaves open.

name: draft-das-agentic-effectuation-boundary
title: When AI Agents Hold the Keys: Threat Model and Execution-Finality Requirements for Autonomous High-Consequence Systems
abstract: AI agents are increasingly being delegated authority to invoke APIs,    move money, modify enterprise state, operate infrastructure, and    trigger physical actions.  Existing mechanisms for authentication,    authorization, proof-of-possession, attestation, request    preconditions, and authorization-context propagation are necessary    building blocks, but they do not by themselves establish a universal    invariant that the exact consequential act approved earlier is the    exact act permitted to become effective now.     This document defines a threat model for autonomous high-consequence    agents and identifies an effectuation-boundary gap: a request can be    correctly authenticated, correctly authorized, correctly attested,    and still be unsafe to execute because parameters, policy state,    external prerequisites, delegation state, lineage, or the execution    path changed after the earlier decision.  The document describes an    execution-finality architecture in which a proposed act remains non-    effective until a protected enforcement point verifies exact-act    binding, freshness, current policy state, anti-replay state, required    provenance, and path completeness immediately before effectuation,    with authority consumed in coordination with the consequential    commit.

name: draft-das-agentic-execution-finality
title: Tool Selection Is Not Execution: Finality for Agentic Tool Dispatch in High-Risk AI Systems
abstract: This architecture is specifically designed for high-risk AI systems,    where standard engineering priorities shift from speed and latency    toward absolute determinism and safety.     An agentic model can emit a tool call that today's runtimes treat as    something to execute.  Allowlists, OAuth tokens, MCP server auth,    sandboxes, output filters, and human approval decide whether an agent    may reach a tool.  They do not decide whether this generated call,    with this argument digest, from this instruction chain, at this    delegation depth, may take effect now.     That gap is the incident surface.  Prompt-injected content, poisoned    retrieval, a malicious tool response, or a delegated sub-agent can    produce a call that looks like ordinary tool use.  If the dispatcher    executes whatever the model selected, policy that lived upstream    becomes advisory.     This document specifies a dispatch-time gate.  The model may compute    a call.  The call remains a Candidate Act. A Protected Enforcement    Domain binds agent, tool, arguments, purpose, destination,    provenance, and policy epochs, then issues scoped non-bearer    authority.  A Tool-Dispatch Finality Sink verifies that authority    against the actual invocation immediately before the tool runs, then    consumes it.  The same gate applies to support, coding, payments,    clinical, SOC, browser-use, and multi-agent MCP deployments.  Tool    selection is not execution authority.     A runnable reference implementation for this dispatch-time gate is    provided at tool_use Is Not invoke(): Binding Execution-Finality to    Agentic Tool-Call Interfaces and MCP (https://github.com/sangmdas/    tool_use-Is-Not-invoke-Binding-Execution-Finality-to-Agentic-Tool-    Call-Interfaces-and-MCP).

name: draft-das-agentic-tool-binding
title: tool_use Is Not invoke(): Binding Execution-Finality to Agentic Tool-Call Interfaces and MCP
abstract: Frontier runtimes already standardized the dangerous moment.  A model    emits a tool_use block, a tool_calls array, or an MCP tools/call    payload.  The host then invokes whatever name and arguments the model    printed.  Alignment, allowlists, and OAuth sit around that moment.    They do not sit on it.     The consequence of this gap is no longer confined to email or payment    demos.  In defense, energy, grid control, industrial process control,    and other critical-infrastructure deployments, the same tool_use    block already reaches actuation-class systems -- logistics and    targeting-adjacent decision support, SCADA and PLC interfaces,    medical devices, autonomous platforms.  In these environments,    detection after the fact is not mitigation; it is an incident report    written after the effect has already occurred.  An agent that can act    at machine speed but cannot be halted at machine speed is a system    running without brakes: the first uncontrolled invocation is not a    warning sign, it is the accident.  Command authority, human    oversight, and legal review all operate on human time.  An unbound    tool_use block operates on machine time.  When those two clocks    diverge, the gap belongs to whichever side reaches the effect first    -- and today, nothing structurally guarantees that side is    authorization.     This document does not invent another assistant API.  It binds the    Agent Candidate Act profile [I-D.das-agentic] onto the three    interface families those runtimes and their customers already ship:    tool_use / computer_use style interfaces, function-calling and    structured tool-response interfaces, and Model Context Protocol    tools/call.  The model may emit the block.  The block remains non-    effective.  A local enforcer builds the act, binds the argument    digest, and refuses invoke() until scoped authority is verified and    consumed at the dispatch sink.     For consequence classes above a defined threshold -- FINANCIAL,    PHYSICAL, NETWORK_CONTROL, and any act reaching defense or critical-    infrastructure actuation -- this binding treats fail-closed as the    only conforming behavior: absent successfully verified, current, act-    bound authority, the candidate act stays non-effective regardless of    model confidence, prior session trust, or upstream alignment signal.    Each enforcement decision, allow or deny, commits a Ledger-Anchored    Validation Receipt (LAVR) -- a signed, hash-chained enforcement    artifact bound to the specific candidate act and its argument digest    at the moment of decision.  An LAVR is not a log entry assembled    afterward for audit; it is the proof that the finality boundary    actually gated this act before any effect could occur, and its    absence is itself a fail-closed condition.     The implementation target is a middleware function that a host loop    can call without changing the model vendor. tool_use is not invoke().

name: draft-das-ai-factory-silicon-finality
title: Execution Finality for AI-Factory Silicon and Accelerated Infrastructure: Enforcement Profiles for GPUs, Chiplets, Memory Fabrics, DPUs, RDMA, CXL, and Photonic Boundaries
abstract: AI factories and AI-native infrastructure are heterogeneous control    systems in which CPUs, GPUs, NPUs, memory controllers, CXL and PCIe    paths, DMA and RDMA engines, DPUs, SmartNICs, accelerator fabrics,    chiplets, storage, optical interconnects, model-serving runtimes,    schedulers, firmware, and physical power or cooling controllers can    all participate in one consequential operation.  Existing industry    mechanisms such as authentication, access control, workload identity,    attestation, confidential computing, IOMMU/SMMU isolation, memory    protection, transport security, scheduler policy, safety logic, and    hardware roots of trust are necessary building blocks, but they do    not by themselves define one common rule for whether the exact    pending operation is still authorized at the instant and location    where it becomes effective.     This document describes that missing effectuation-boundary rule.  In    plain engineering terms, the architecture holds a consequential    operation in a pending or inhibited state, identifies the exact    command, transfer, route, memory range, output, configuration change,    or actuation request, validates current authority and protected    state, binds a narrowly scoped authorization artifact to those exact    parameters and to the intended enforcement boundary, and requires the    boundary that physically or logically controls the consequence to    verify the binding before commit.  The boundary therefore acts like a    policy enforcement point, reference monitor, transaction-commit gate,    command gate, safety interlock, actuation gate, output-release gate,    or hardware admission controller, depending on the deployment domain.     The document uses the specialized terms Candidate Act, Non-Effective    State, Protected Enforcement Domain, Protected Validation Evidence,    scoped non-bearer capability, and Finality Sink.  These terms name    functions rather than required products or protocol objects.    Equivalent implementations may instead use concepts such as a staged    transaction, command descriptor, authorization decision record,    sender-constrained or context-bound permit, anti-replay state,    generation or fencing epoch, compare-and-swap style commit, fail-safe    inhibit, or transactional check-and-commit.  The functional    requirement is that the actual pending effect cannot complete through    the protected path unless the exact act, current state, freshness,    scope, destination, and effectuation boundary still correspond.     The Finality Sink is the component with mandatory control over the    consequence.  Depending on the profile, it may be a memory    controller, HBM gate, GPU scheduler, accelerator partition    controller, IOMMU or SMMU, DMA or RDMA engine, DPU or SmartNIC,    fabric switch, chiplet link controller, CXL component, cache-    coherence controller, model loader, token-emission gate, optical    modulator or wavelength controller, eFPGA configuration gate, rack    power controller, radio-control path, or another protected commit    point.  Physical separation from the compute component is not    required; mandatory mediation and protected verification are    required.     The document provides 98 detailed Enforcement Profiles.  Sixty-three    translate the supplied GPU, silicon, chiplet, memory-fabric, and AI-    factory source set; twelve supplementary profiles map the same    execution-finality model onto current hyperscale and Arm-based    infrastructure directions; eight additional profiles selectively    adapt non-duplicative mechanisms from companion DAS Protocols    disclosures for silicon and AI-factory use; and fifteen profiles    address electrical package-I/O, sideband, error, test, and coherence-    transition boundaries.  Profile identifiers retain source numbering    for traceability, so gaps are intentional.     The architecture is intended to complement, not replace, accelerated    computing, confidential computing, chiplet and coherent-memory    protocols, accelerator fabrics, optical I/O, attestation, identity,    authorization, hardware isolation, safety engineering, and existing    control systems.  The IETF relevance is principally the cross-layer    relationship among identity, evidence, attestation, cryptographic    binding, protected state, replay resistance, delegation, and the    final effectuation boundary.  Hardware-specific wire protocols remain    within the remit of the appropriate hardware, semiconductor,    telecommunications, optical, automotive, aerospace, and control-    system standards bodies.  The common invariant is: computation may    produce a proposed act, but computation alone is not authority for    consequence.

name: draft-das-ai-native-6g-execution-finality
title: Execution-Finality for AI-Native 5G/6G and O-RAN
abstract: In programmable and AI-assisted mobile networks, successful    authentication of a network function or AI controller does not    establish authority for every routing, signaling, session, resource-    allocation, sensing, or subscriber-specific consequence that the    function can generate.     This document defines an informational execution-finality profile for    AI-native 5G, 5G-Advanced, IMT-2030/6G, O-RAN, and AI-RAN    environments.  A proposed network operation is represented as a    Network Candidate Act and remains in a Non-Effective State while a    Protected Enforcement Domain validates act-specific predicates.    Protected validation evidence is committed before, or atomically    with, release of scoped non-bearer finality authority.  A Network    Finality Sink at the enforcement boundary independently verifies that    authority immediately before live network state changes.     The governing rule is that network authentication is not network    finality, and computation is not authority.  This revision also    defines a JSON interoperability profile for Candidate Acts,    validation decisions, scoped authority, and sink verification.     This profile is distinct from, and complementary to, present AI-    native 6G industry roadmaps that focus on radio, sensing, and    platform capability, including air-interface, MIMO, spectrum, and AI-    RAN infrastructure work described in Qualcomm's public AI-native 6G    platform material, and the broad native-trustworthiness and agentic-    core-network architectures described in Huawei's public 6G security    research.  Those efforts address how a network becomes more    intelligent, autonomous, and platform-trustworthy.  This document    addresses a narrower and later question: once an already-    authenticated, already-policy-approved AI-generated network operation    has been computed, whether that exact operation may become a live    network consequence.  The Candidate Act, Non-Effective State,    Protected Enforcement Domain, and Finality Sink constructs defined    here, as an explicit pre-effectuation gate with act-bound non-bearer    authority and independent sink-side re-verification, are not    established as an equivalent primitive in publicly reviewed material    from those roadmaps.

name: draft-das-ai-safety-evidence-consistency-profiles
title: AI Safety and Operational Consistency: Shared Evidence Semantics and Domain-Specific Profiles
abstract: Part 01 of 15 defines a cross-domain evidence-consistency framework    for AI-related operations in distributed software,    telecommunications, device processing, autonomous commerce, and    physical systems.  It addresses operation identity, source-qualified    observations, resource and policy generations, temporal    applicability, uncertain effects, and versioned reassessment.  The    common framework is a method for expressing and evaluating evidence    obligations, not a universal execution protocol or a claim that    different physical and network systems share one control mechanism.     An outer three-valued classification (SUPPORTED, CONTRADICTED,    UNRESOLVED) is scoped to a declared verification objective.  Each    domain defines its own predicates, measurement contracts, control    authorities, response-time bounds, and effect semantics.  In    particular, verified observation consistency does not itself    establish authority to execute, cryptographic safety of a device    descriptor, completion of a telecommunications settlement, or    physical safety of robot motion.     The document specifies a layered integration approach: reusable    evidence and outcome semantics, twelve independently implementable    domain profiles, and optional typed interfaces between profiles when    a genuine cross-system dependency exists.  It compares conventional    controls with specific remaining problems, describes conditional    benefits and incompatibilities, and provides analytical rather than    measured latency and resource models.     The remaining fourteen parts detail radio control, incident recovery,    session and charging lifecycle, hardware observation, multi-agent    agreements, asynchronous tools, robotic capability, multilingual    instructions, browser actions, runtime migration, autonomous    commerce, silicon command processing, protected egress, and cross-    interface operation control.  This foundation provides search-    oriented descriptions of 639 engineering mechanisms and links to    their specialist explanations; the profiles are not assumed to be    interchangeable or automatically composable.

name: draft-das-ai-safety-network-incident-recovery
title: AI Safety for Multi-Agent Network Incident Diagnosis, Coordinated Repair, and Outcome Verification
abstract: Part 03 of 15 addresses AI safety in multi-agent network incident    diagnosis, evidence-qualified root-cause assessment, coordinated    remediation, asynchronous repair, and operational recovery    verification.  It distinguishes independent network observations from    repeated derivative reports, competing diagnostic hypotheses from    established faults, plan acceptance from actual configuration    effects, and successful interventions from verified network-service    recovery.  Group B workflow B-CW-01 and six detailed embodiments    address incident identity, source-qualified provenance, cascading    cross-domain faults, concurrent interventions, partial repair,    compensation, recurrence, and incident handoff.  Consistency    assessments are distinct from authority to change network resources.    The foundational Part 01 provides shared evidence and state    semantics; Parts 02, 04, 07, 11, 14, and 15 describe complementary    radio, service, asynchronous, continuity, and protected-operation    mechanisms.  The appendix provides direct navigation across all    fifteen parts.     The technical problem is that conventional event aggregation and    change orchestration can report a coherent incident diagnosis or    completed repair without proving the independence, timing or scope of    supporting observations or actual restoration of the intended    service.  This part describes evidence-qualified three-valued    conclusions, separate operation admission, post-repair effect    verification, implementation profiles, explicit failure paths and    source-preserving recovery history.  A runnable Python laboratory    supplies synthetic reproducible tests and local processing    measurements; it is not an operational network performance    demonstration.  It complements Part 01 shared evidence semantics and    Part 02 radio observation qualification where incident decisions    depend on radio telemetry.

name: draft-das-ai-safety-radio-observation-consistency
title: AI Safety for Radio Network Observation and Control Calculation Consistency
abstract: Part 02 of 15 describes AI safety for distributed radio-access-    network observation and control calculation consistency.  A radio    controller may receive independently valid telemetry that is jointly    unsuitable for the same calculation because it refers to different    cell or beam identities, configuration generations, clock domains,    acquisition intervals, measurement units, aggregation semantics, or    shared upstream evidence.  This document develops A-CW-01 and six    specialized procedures for source-qualified temporal consistency,    resource reassignment, measurement transformation, dependency-aware    observation selection, coupled multi-resource decisions, and    controller failover.  It specifies evidence-scoped supported,    contradicted, and unresolved outcomes, with revalidation after    material state changes.  The result qualifies a calculation; it does    not independently authorize modification of live radio resources.    Companion Parts 01, 03, 04, 05, 11, and 14 address shared evidence    semantics, network recovery, service state, hardware observations,    migration, and optional protected effectuation boundaries.

name: draft-das-ai-safety-telecom-session-lifecycle
title: AI Safety for Telecommunications Session, Resource, Usage, and Charging State Consistency
abstract: Part 04 of 15 describes Group C mechanisms for evidence-qualified    reconstruction of subscriber trust, telecommunications session    identity, home and visited operator state, programmable quality-of-    service operation, resource reservation and installation, user-plane    metering, charging, accounting, and deferred settlement.  It    distinguishes an accepted API request from an installed network    resource, a subscriber trust change from session release, a usage    report from a financial obligation, and a local release from complete    session closure.  It includes C-CW-01, six specialist embodiments,    formal mathematics, flowcharts, and source-linked technical    checkpoints.  Part 01 supplies common evidence and consistency    semantics, while Parts 02, 03, 07, 11, 12, 14, and 15 cover    complementary radio observations, incident repair, asynchronous    processing, continuity, commerce, and protected operation boundaries.    Positive observation consistency does not itself authorize    consequential network actuation.     The technical gap arises when individually valid subscriber, roaming,    service, metering and charging records cannot be shown to apply to    the same operation, generation, time and verified outcome.  This    document specifies a source-qualified lifecycle graph with typed non-    equivalent states, scoped three-valued evidence decisions, late-    record correction, separate authority and effect-observation    boundaries, practical implementation profiles, and failure/edge    cases.  Nine source-derived RFCXML diagrams are explained in the    body.  A standard-library Python reference and 87 synthetic tests    illustrate selected in-memory algorithms; measured evaluator timings    are not network latency, not peer reviewed and not field validation.    Part 01 supplies shared evidence semantics; Parts 02, 03, 05, 07, 11,    12, 14 and 15 address complementary inputs, failures and    consequential effects.

name: draft-das-cross-platform-ai-interoperability
title: Secure AI Execution-Finality for iOS, Android, and Cross-Platform AI Agents, Part 2: Secure iOS and Android AI Tool Interoperability
abstract: AI assistants and third-party AI tools now act across the Apple and    Google ecosystems.  Apple Siri invokes app actions through App    Intents and Shortcuts, Google Gemini acts through Android intents and    app integrations, and agents from many vendors reach the same    accounts from iOS, iPadOS, macOS, Android, Windows, Linux, cloud    APIs, and connected devices.  Each hop crosses a different    permission, sandbox, credential, identity, and hardware trust model.    A prompt-injected, replayed, or redirected tool call can then export    a file, send a payment, change data, or operate a device in a way    that differs from what the user approved, and app permissions,    Keychain or Android Keystore credentials, and OAuth tokens do not by    themselves prove that the executed operation matches the approved    one.     This document, Part 2 of a twelve-part series, specifies how to carry    authority across platforms without letting a platform permission    become final authority.  Platform-specific adapters for iOS and    Android translate qualified app, user, device, and key evidence into    a protected canonical effect descriptor; the AI tool's proposed    action remains non-effective; operation-scoped, non-bearer    authorization resists replay and redirection; and the receiving    Finality Sink independently reconstructs the actual pending    operation, checks resource identity, aliases, and redirects, fences    stale devices after cross-device handoff, and fails closed on any    mismatch.  Reference data models, pseudocode, a state machine, six    threat models, and twenty reproducible validation tests are included.    Part 1 of the series defines the shared terminology and common    workflows.     The document relates these mechanisms to OAuth 2.0 Rich Authorization    Requests and Demonstrating Proof of Possession (DPoP); Workload    Identity in Multi-System Environments (WIMSE); Remote ATtestation    procedureS (RATS); CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE);    Authentication and Authorization for Constrained Environments (ACE);    Supply Chain Integrity, Transparency, and Trust (SCITT); and HTTP    redirection and conditional requests.  It identifies discussion    points for these groups and for Security Area dispatch, without    claiming working-group adoption or IETF consensus.     Industry alignment covers Apple iOS, iPadOS, and macOS with Siri, App    Intents, and Shortcuts; Google Android with Intents, Binder, and    Android Keystore; Google Gemini; Samsung Bixby; Microsoft Windows and    Azure agent governance; agent platforms from OpenAI, Anthropic, and    Meta; NVIDIA, Qualcomm, Arm, and Huawei hardware; and payments,    telecommunications, and robotics.  Product names are illustrative and    imply no endorsement or implementation by any vendor.  For the EU    Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), operation-    level evidence and fail-closed cross-platform enforcement can help    providers and deployers address risk-management, record-keeping,    human-oversight, and robustness and cybersecurity requirements where    those obligations apply; this is a technical mapping, not a    conformity claim or legal advice.

name: draft-das-distributed-agent-authority-finality
title: Distributed Authority and Execution-Finality for Multi-Agent Systems, Delegated Operations, and Cross-Domain Gateways
abstract: This informational document describes future-oriented distributed    authority and execution-finality profiles for cooperating autonomous    agents, delegated operations, external tools, cloud gateways, native    resources, and cross-domain workflows.  It examines identity, non-    amplifying delegation, provenance and influence lineage, transitive    side effects, cross-agent collision management, policy convergence    and downstream effectuation-boundary enforcement.  It distinguishes a    proposed objective or authorized plan from authority for an actual    resource effect.  Source-derived procedures, tests and algorithms are    presented as implementation examples, not as evidence that identified    vendors implement this proposed architecture.     Industry Relevance: Recent public developments in autonomous AI-agent    security and execution governance include Microsoft Execution    Containers (MXC), Microsoft Agent Governance Toolkit ADR-0030    (Action-Bound, Fail-Closed Approval Protocol), and Project    Perception; Google Agent Gateway and Gemini Agent; Meta Muse/Sentinel    AI-Agent Security Architecture; NVIDIA OpenShell Reference    Architecture and NVIDIA Sentry; OpenAI Agents API, Codex, Agents SDK,    and Responses API; and Anthropic Claude Managed Agents, Claude Code    Sandboxing, and Claude Code Auto Mode.  These initiatives illustrate    industry attention to agent isolation, independent policy    enforcement, action-bound authorization, delegated authority,    credential isolation, network-egress security, hardware-assisted    containment, runtime supervision, and fail-closed controls.  This    draft describes related proposed execution-finality mechanisms    without asserting that these initiatives implement them.     Relevance to the IETF: the mechanisms described here require common,    interoperable objects and verification semantics across independently    built components, including operation descriptors, act-bound non-    bearer capabilities, finality-sink verification results, validation    evidence, and authority, revocation, and containment generations.    The document relates to existing IETF work on OAuth, GNAP, RATS,    WIMSE, and SCITT, and asks the community whether and where this    effectuation-boundary problem should be addressed.     This document is intentionally long and is not repetitive: each    profile specifies a distinct mechanism with its own algorithms,    failure cases, and enforcement points, and the security properties    depend on how these mechanisms combine.  A reduced excerpt would hide    the conditions under which they fail closed, so this document and its    two companion drafts, among which the profiles are divided, are meant    to be evaluated as a whole.     This draft builds on earlier Internet-Drafts by the same author, in    particular draft-das-agent-execution-finality, and adds mechanism    families not described there; the Introduction states precisely what    was disclosed earlier and what is disclosed here.     IPR: The technical content of this draft set is based upon the    author's international application PCT/IB2026/055615, which forms the    foundation of this disclosure and comprises approximately 300    distinct, non-repetitive embodiments and enforcement points.  A    separate patent application specific to the material in this draft    set has also been filed.  Related Indian applications: 202531130665,    202631000572, 202631001586, 202631002990, 202631124028, and    202631125689.  Related international applications: PCT/IB2025/058316,    PCT/IB2026/053385, PCT/IB2026/055615, PCT/IB2026/055760, PCT/    IB2026/055870, PCT/IB2026/056058, PCT/IB2026/056809, and PCT/    IB2026/056941.  These identify related technical disclosures; not all    described mechanisms are necessarily patent-claimed or granted, and    patent scope and priority depend on applicable law and examination.

name: draft-das-enterprise-ai-enforcement-profiles
title: Securing the Enterprise Future: Technical Non-Joinability for Enterprise AI
abstract: Enterprise artificial-intelligence systems are increasingly connected    to multiple organizational repositories, applications, tools, memory    systems, and workflow interfaces.  Representative industrial    deployment classes include OpenAI ChatGPT and ChatGPT Work, Anthropic    Claude, Google Gemini Enterprise, xAI Grok for Business, Microsoft    Copilot and Copilot Studio, Amazon Q Business, Salesforce Agentforce,    ServiceNow AI Agents, and comparable enterprise or privately deployed    AI systems.  These names are cited only as publicly described    examples of the broader deployment class.  Their inclusion does not    assert that any named product implements, lacks, requires, endorses,    or is vulnerable to the mechanisms described here, does not    characterize undisclosed internal architectures, and does not imply    that equivalent functionality is absent from an existing product or    specification.     The security problem considered here is not limited to theft of a    pre-existing database.  An enterprise-AI workload may be individually    authorized to retrieve information from customer, engineering,    financial, source-code, supplier, scheduling, communication, memory,    and operational systems while the combination of those sources    reveals a sensitive relationship or future enterprise state that no    single repository contains.  Conventional access control, encryption,    network segmentation, database separation, confidential computing,    and source-level authorization remain important, but storage    separation alone does not prevent such reconstruction where the same    effective authority can obtain the constituent values and freely    resolve the relationships among them.     The mechanism described here therefore separates not only protected    data but also the authority required to create protected semantic    relationships among that data.
